notes.definition: Living organisms are organised in levels: cells are the basic building blocks, a tissue is a group of cells with a similar structure and function, organs are groups of tissues performing a specific function, and organs work together in organ systems that form whole organisms.
explanation: Large multicellular organisms such as humans and flowering plants contain many millions of cells. These cells are not all the same. During development, cells differentiate (become specialised) so that each type has a structure suited to a particular job. Specialisation means work can be divided up, which makes a large organism more efficient than a single cell trying to do everything.

A tissue is a group of cells with a similar structure and function. Examples in animals are muscular tissue, which contracts to bring about movement; glandular tissue, which makes and releases substances such as enzymes and hormones; and epithelial tissue, which covers the outside and lines the inside of organs. In plants, examples include epidermal tissue, palisade mesophyll and xylem.

An organ is an aggregation (a collection) of different tissues that work together to perform a specific function. The stomach is an organ: muscular tissue churns the food, glandular tissue produces digestive juices containing enzymes and hydrochloric acid, and epithelial tissue covers the inside and outside. The leaf, the heart and the brain are other examples of organs.

An organ system is a group of organs that work together to carry out a particular function. The digestive system (including the salivary glands, oesophagus, stomach, liver, pancreas, small intestine and large intestine) digests and absorbs food. Other examples include the circulatory system, the breathing system and, in plants, the transport system made up of roots, stems and leaves.

Organ systems do not work alone. They work together to form a whole organism. For example, the digestive system supplies glucose and the breathing system supplies oxygen, while the circulatory system carries both to every cell so it can respire. Thinking in terms of scale helps: a cell is measured in micrometres (μm), a tissue may be a fraction of a millimetre thick, an organ is measured in centimetres and an organism may be over a metre tall.
keyFacts: Cells are the basic building blocks of all living organisms.
A tissue is a group of cells with a similar structure and function.
An organ is a collection of different tissues that perform a specific function.
An organ system is a group of organs that work together to perform a function.
Organ systems work together to form organisms.
Order of increasing complexity: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.
The stomach contains muscular, glandular and epithelial tissue.
The leaf is a plant organ; roots, stems and leaves form a plant organ system.
1 mm = 1000 μm, so most cells are far smaller than a millimetre.

keyTerms.definition: The basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms.
A group of cells with a similar structure and function.
A collection of different tissues working together to perform a specific function.
A group of organs that work together to carry out a particular function.
A whole living thing made of organ systems working together.
A cell that has differentiated to have a structure adapted to a particular function.
Tissue that covers the outside of the body and lines organs.
Tissue that produces and secretes substances such as enzymes and hormones.

workedExamples.title: Placing structures in the hierarchy
workedExamples.question: Classify each of these as a cell, tissue, organ or organ system: red blood cell, heart, xylem, digestive system.
steps: A red blood cell is a single specialised cell, so it is a cell.
The heart contains muscular tissue, nervous tissue and connective tissue working together, so it is an organ.
Xylem is made of many similar cells that together transport water, so it is a tissue.
The digestive system contains many organs (stomach, intestines, pancreas) working together, so it is an organ system.
workedExamples.answer: Red blood cell: cell. Heart: organ. Xylem: tissue. Digestive system: organ system.

workedExamples.title: Size and scale
workedExamples.question: A layer of epithelial tissue is 0.06 mm thick. Each cell in the layer is 15 μm thick. How many cells thick is the layer?
steps: Convert the tissue thickness to micrometres: 0.06 mm × 1000 = 60 μm.
Divide by the thickness of one cell: 60 ÷ 15 = 4.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a tissue and an organ are the same thing.
misconceptions.right: In fact a tissue is a group of similar cells, while an organ is made of several different tissues working together.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think an organ contains only one type of tissue.
misconceptions.right: In fact organs such as the stomach contain several types of tissue, for example muscular, glandular and epithelial tissue.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think plants do not have organs or organ systems.
misconceptions.right: In fact leaves, stems and roots are plant organs, and together they form an organ system for transporting substances.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think organ systems work independently.
misconceptions.right: In fact organ systems depend on each other; for example the circulatory system transports the products of the digestive and breathing systems.

realWorld: Organ transplants replace a whole organ, such as a kidney or heart, because the organ's tissues must work together to do its job.
Tissue engineering grows tissues such as skin in the laboratory to treat severe burns.
Doctors take biopsies (small samples of tissue) to examine cells under a microscope and diagnose disease.
examTips: Learn the definitions word for word: 'a tissue is a group of cells with a similar structure and function' is what examiners look for.
When asked to order levels, always start with the cell and finish with the organism: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.
If asked why something is an organ, say it contains more than one type of tissue and name them if you can.
In size and scale questions, convert all lengths to the same unit first (usually μm), remembering 1 mm = 1000 μm.
summary: Cells are the basic building blocks of living organisms.
Tissues are groups of cells with a similar structure and function.
Organs are made of different tissues working together.
Organ systems are groups of organs working together.
Organ systems work together to make an organism.
The stomach (muscular, glandular, epithelial tissue) is a classic example of an organ.

questions.question: Which of these is the definition of a tissue?
options: A group of organs working together
A group of cells with a similar structure and function
A single cell that carries out one job
questions.explanation: A tissue is made of similar cells doing the same job. A group of organs working together is an organ system.

questions.question: Which list shows the levels of organisation in order of increasing complexity?
options: Cell, organ, tissue, organ system, organism
Tissue, cell, organ, organism, organ system
Cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism
Organism, organ system, organ, tissue, cell
questions.explanation: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems and organ systems form organisms. Option D is the right sequence but in decreasing complexity.

questions.question: Which of these is an organ?
questions.explanation: The stomach contains several tissues. A red blood cell is a cell, muscular tissue is a tissue and the digestive system is an organ system.

questions.question: Which of these is an organ system?
questions.explanation: The circulatory system is made of the heart, blood and blood vessels working together. The leaf and heart are organs; xylem is a tissue.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a section through the wall of the stomach.
Tissue X produces digestive juices.
Which type of tissue is X?
questions.explanation: Glandular tissue secretes digestive juices containing enzymes and acid. Muscular tissue churns the contents and epithelial tissue covers and lines the stomach.

questions.question: What is the function of muscular tissue in the stomach?
options: To churn the food and digestive juices together
To absorb glucose into the blood
To cover the inside of the stomach
questions.explanation: Muscle contracts to churn the stomach contents. Acid is made by glandular tissue, and the stomach is not the main site of absorption.

questions.question:
Xylem is made of many similar cells that transport water and mineral ions.
Which level of organisation is xylem?
questions.explanation: Xylem is made of many similar cells that all transport water and mineral ions, so it is a tissue.

questions.question: Why is a leaf classed as an organ?
options: It is made of a single type of cell
It contains several different tissues that work together
It is part of the transport system
questions.explanation: An organ is defined by containing different tissues working together. Having chloroplasts or being part of a system does not by itself make something an organ.

questions.question:
A student wrote:
'Blood is an organ because it contains several types of cell.'
Which statement best corrects the student's error?
options: Blood is an organ system because it travels to all organs
Blood is a tissue because its cells and plasma work together to transport substances
Blood is a cell because red blood cells are its main component
Blood is not living so it is not part of any level of organisation
questions.explanation: Blood is classed as a tissue: a group of cells (with plasma) working together for transport. An organ is made of several different tissues, not just several types of cell.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why large multicellular organisms need organ systems?
options: Each cell can carry out every function equally well
Organ systems increase the number of chromosomes in each cell
Organ systems are needed only for reproduction
Specialised cells grouped into tissues, organs and systems allow functions to be carried out efficiently and substances to be exchanged and transported over large distances
questions.explanation: Specialisation with division of labour makes a large organism efficient; systems such as the circulatory system link cells that are far from the surface.

questions.question: Convert 2.5 mm into micrometres (μm).

Table 1 shows the length of one muscle cell and the length of a piece of muscular tissue.
Calculate how many muscle cells, placed end to end, would fit along the piece of muscular tissue.

headers: Length of one muscle cell in μm
Length of muscular tissue in mm

questions.explanation: Convert to the same units first: 4 mm = 4000 μm. Then 4000 ÷ 50 = 80 cells. Forgetting to convert gives 0.08, which is impossible.

questions.question:
The lining of the small intestine is made of epithelial tissue, one cell thick.
Figure 1 shows a villus from the small intestine.
Calculate how many times taller the villus is than one epithelial cell.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a section through the wall of the stomach.
Calculate the percentage of the thickness of the stomach wall that is muscular tissue.
questions.explanation: Percentage = part ÷ whole × 100 = 3.5 ÷ 5 × 100 = 70%.
questions.answerLabel: Percentage of wall that is muscular tissue

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the number of cells in a human body.
Calculate the percentage of body cells that are red blood cells.
Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
questions.explanation: 2.5 ÷ 3.7 = 0.6757, × 100 = 67.57%, which is 68% to 2 significant figures. The powers of ten cancel because both numbers are × 10^13.

questions.question: What is meant by an organ system?
markScheme: 1 mark: a group of organs that work together to perform a particular function
questions.explanation: An organ system is the level above organ: several organs cooperating, for example the digestive system.

questions.question:
Name two different tissues found in the stomach.
Give the function of each tissue.
markScheme: 1 mark: one tissue with correct function (for example muscular tissue churns contents)
1 mark: a second tissue with correct function (for example glandular tissue produces digestive juices / enzymes / acid; epithelial tissue covers or lines the stomach)
questions.explanation: The stomach contains muscular, glandular and epithelial tissue. Each must be paired with its own function.

questions.question: Explain why the heart is described as an organ rather than a tissue.
acceptedAnswers: more than one type of tissue
markScheme: 1 mark: the heart is made of several different tissues (for example muscle, nervous, connective)
1 mark: which work together to perform a specific function (pumping blood)
questions.explanation: A tissue is one type of cell grouping. The heart is an organ because it combines different tissues to perform the job of pumping blood.

questions.question: Give one example of a plant organ.
questions.explanation: Roots, stems and leaves are plant organs; together they form a transport organ system.

questions.question: Describe the difference between a cell and a tissue.
acceptedAnswers: tissue is a group of cells
markScheme: 1 mark: a cell is a single basic unit of life
1 mark: a tissue is a group of (many) cells with a similar structure and function
questions.explanation: Cells are the building blocks; many similar cells together make a tissue.

questions.question:
The digestive system and the circulatory system work together.
Explain how.
markScheme: 1 mark: the digestive system breaks down food into small soluble molecules (such as glucose) and absorbs them into the blood
1 mark: the circulatory system transports these molecules around the body
1 mark: to cells where they are used, for example glucose for respiration or amino acids to build proteins
questions.explanation: Organ systems depend on each other. Absorbed molecules are useless unless the blood delivers them to the cells that need them.

questions.question:
Amoeba is a single-celled organism. It does not have organs.
Suggest why a large multicellular organism, such as a human, needs specialised cells organised into tissues, organs and organ systems.
acceptedAnswers: small surface area to volume ratio
markScheme: 1 mark: humans have a small surface area to volume ratio / cells are far from the surface
1 mark: so diffusion alone is too slow to supply all cells, so exchange surfaces and transport systems (organ systems) are needed
1 mark: specialised cells are adapted to particular functions so they carry them out more efficiently (division of labour)
questions.explanation: Large organisms cannot rely on diffusion across the body surface; organs such as lungs and systems such as the circulatory system solve this, and specialisation improves efficiency.

questions.question:
A doctor removes a small sample of liver for examination.
Table 1 shows the types of cell found in the sample.
Explain whether the sample should be described as a tissue or as part of an organ.

rows: Forms the walls of blood vessels
Lines the tubes that carry bile

markScheme: 1 mark: because it contains several different types of tissue (cells of different structure and function), not just one group of similar cells
questions.explanation: One tissue contains cells with a similar structure and function. A sample containing several different tissues comes from an organ.

questions.question: Which of these is a single cell?
questions.explanation: A root hair cell is one specialised cell. Palisade mesophyll and phloem are tissues; a leaf is an organ.

questions.question: Which organ is part of the digestive system and produces digestive enzymes?
questions.explanation: The pancreas releases enzymes into the small intestine. The lung, heart and kidney belong to other systems.

questions.question: Which row correctly matches each structure to its level of organisation?
options: Guard cell: tissue; epidermis: organ; leaf: organ system
Guard cell: cell; epidermis: organ; leaf: organ
Guard cell: cell; epidermis: tissue; leaf: organ
Guard cell: tissue; epidermis: tissue; leaf: organ
questions.explanation: A guard cell is one cell, the epidermis is a layer of similar cells (a tissue), and the leaf contains several tissues so it is an organ.

questions.question: Describe how cells are organised to form a human organism. Use the digestive system as an example.
markScheme: Indicative content: cells are the basic building blocks; cells differentiate to become specialised; similar cells form tissues, for example muscle cells form muscular tissue; glandular tissue makes enzymes; epithelial tissue lines organs; different tissues form an organ such as the stomach; the stomach, pancreas, liver, small and large intestine work together as the digestive system; organ systems work together to form the organism.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear description of all levels from cell to organism, with a correct digestive example at tissue, organ and system level.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some levels named or correctly ordered, with limited or partly incorrect examples.
questions.explanation: Good answers move through every level in order and give a specific digestive example at each level rather than just listing terms.

questions.question: Explain how the different tissues in the stomach allow it to function as an organ, and explain why the stomach must work with other organs and organ systems to provide cells with the substances they need.
markScheme: Indicative content: muscular tissue contracts to churn food and mix it with digestive juices, increasing contact with enzymes; glandular tissue secretes protease (pepsin) and hydrochloric acid, which kills microorganisms and gives the optimum pH for the protease; epithelial tissue lines and covers the stomach, protecting it; the tissues together carry out the specific function of beginning protein digestion; the stomach alone cannot complete digestion or absorb most products; the pancreas and small intestine complete digestion; the small intestine absorbs small soluble molecules; the circulatory system transports them to cells; the breathing system supplies oxygen for respiration of glucose.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed explanation of each tissue's role linked to the organ's function, and a clear explanation of interaction with other organs and systems.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): roles of at least two tissues explained, with some reference to other organs or systems.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): tissues named or simple statements about the stomach with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Top answers link structure to function at tissue level, then step up to organ system and organism level, showing the full hierarchy.
